newsitem.title: MEXICO: BASEBALL-CARIBBEAN SERIES HERO STARK CHASES A DREAM IN MEXICO.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-CARIBBEAN SERIES HERO STARK CHASES A DREAM IN MEXICO.

text.p: When a shoulder injury and age cost Matt Stark his job as a professional baseball player up north, he headed to Mexico to use his big bat to chase his dream of making it back to the major leagues.

The 32-year-old Stark, who played only briefly for the Toronto Blue Jays in 1987 and the Chicgo White Sox in 1990, is a long way from the major leagues. In fact, as a designated hitter these days with Tomateros de Culiacan (Culiacan Tomato Growers), he says he feels the big leagues up north have forgotten all about him.
But in the recent Caribbean Series against teams loaded with major league talent, Stark reminded everyone that he's still around.

At first it did not appear that Stark would get many quality at bats in the Series. He began the six-day, four-nation tournament on the bench, after his team, representing Mexico, picked up reinforcements from the rest of the Mexican Pacific League.
But Stark proved he was not washed up yet.
In the Series, which ended Sunday, Stark hit four clutch home runs and was named the Most Valuable player.
He came off the bench to pinch hit a home run in the ninth inning against Venezuela to tie the game. Mexico went on to win it.

The next day he hit two home runs. A two-run shot in the first inning gave Mexico a 2-0 lead, and a solo homer in the seventh off Pat Mahomes, a former Minnesota Twins player, gave Mexico a 6-4 lead. Mexico won the game 10-6 to set up a showdown with the Dominican Republic for the title.

In the championship game, with Mexico down 4-1 in the eighth inning, Stark belted a two-run homer off Dominican closer Dario Veras, also of the San Diego Padres, to pull Mexico to within 4-3. But the Mexico rally died, and The Dominican Republic won the game and the Series.
In his hotel room after the final game, Stark sat next to his MVP trophy, nibbled on a pizza, nursed a Diet Coke and talked about his baseball oddysey.
He said the California Angels released him from their Double-A Midland team in 1991 after leading the Texas League in hitting after the first month of the season.
He was 27 then and recovering from surgery on his throwing shoulder. But the Angels had some younger catching prospects who needed playing time, Stark said.
"I never think about the reasons why things happen," Stark said. "You gotta go on. The opportunity (to play in Mexico) was there and I didn't have a job, so I said, 'let's do it.'"

Since then he has become one of the best hitters in Mexico, batting more than .320 in the Mexican summer league and about .280 in the more competitive winter league, he said. In 1993 with the Mexico City Red Devils he hit 36 home runs.
The numbers he remembers best, of course, were from his brief stints in the majors.
"I'm 5-for-28," he rattled off when asked about his lifetime batting average. "In 1987 I went one for 12 and in 1990 I was four for 16. Not what you'd call quality," he added with a chuckle.

Stark is an imposing figure at 6-foot-4 (1.9 meters) and 250 pounds (113 kg), which he admits is about 25 pounds (11 kg) too much. But he has a short, compact swing, making him a good contact hitter often used to start a hit-and-run.

As for getting back to the majors, his problem, apart from his age, is not playing a regular position. He came up with the Blue Jays as a catcher but has played very little behind the plate in Mexico, where teams pay him for his bat. He also plays a little first base.

"I had seen him when he was a young player way back in (minor-league) A ball but hadn't followed his career for a while. But seeing him here, I remembered right away," said Dominican Manager Mike Quade, who also coaches in the Oakland Athletics minor league system.
"I'm 32 and maybe it's too late," Stark said, "but there's not a great depth of catching in the Major Legues right now, and I've been there. I think I could help somebody."

"It was a pleasure playing against some of these major leaguers," he said, referring to the Caribbean Series, which included teams from the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and Puerto Rico stocked with numerous current major league stars.
"My skills aren't the same as they were 10 years ago, but I still think I have something left if someone would give me the chance.
"I mean, I'll go to rookie ball," he said. "I'll go anywhere."
